C01.note: High: a person grants tonight's powers by merging a file, code holds the agent to them, and the dark phone at 03:12 is the best hands-off scene here that is not a release gate. Low if the night start through the Flows API relay does not really run, or the orders read as auto-rollback with paperwork.

C02.note: The sleep scene and the rule that the model can only add urgency are strong, but the agent never acts, so GitLab and Duo depth is thin for a hands-off claim. Higher if each page arrives with one prepared manual job, as in Wake Budget.

C03.note: Testing fixes on no-traffic Cloud Run revisions is natural Google Cloud use, and the agent runs real experiments instead of chatting. Lower if the replay of a planted bug looks rigged or the incident status trigger does not fire.

C04.note: Customers as the alarm, a reproduction decided by code and a new synthetic check MR close the loop well. Lower because the start rests on a scheduled count of bot-created Service Desk issues, and the check sits near post-deploy verification.

C05.note: Rare and real: nobody owns the 3am leftovers, and it reads incidents, flag history, silences and scaling, with the sponge count as a memorable ritual. Lower if the audit history our token can read is thin and the staged mitigations look scripted.

C06.note: Replaying a rule against history before approval is honest configure-stage work, but it needs weeks of metric and paging history that will be seeded, so the result looks staged on video.

C07.note: A real environment and runbook fix MRs as output, but judges will file it under onboarding aids (36 in June), and a fault toggle can look like a toy.

C08.note: A lovely two-clock scene, but two stages, unverified reads of time zone and status, an outside timer and several accounts. Little GitLab automation to show.

C09.note: Flags that climb only in daylight is a real configure-stage story, but code does the rollout and the model's share is small, so Duo is not at the core, and two days must be time-compressed.

C10.note: Ana's flight to her sister's wedding is one of the best human beats here, but it reads as organizational memory next to LORE, and the automation is mostly mentions and a card on a release.

C11.note: Running old code on the new schema is a real check few tools automate, and the split MR is a fix, not a verdict. Lower because it lives in the release gate space beside BABYDOV's rollback rehearsal, and migration plumbing can eat the build.

C12.note: The most GitLab-native human loop in the pool: Service Desk, a feature flag user list in production, replies read back, a person widens, then a release. Lower only if pitched as a 'your bug is fixed' email, which collides with the banned notifier and Proof of Fix.

C13.note: The strongest 30 seconds here (Maria hearing 'button, button, button') and a truly agentic use: the model drives a keyboard like a screen reader user. Lower on stages, and if the browser cannot run in the flow sandbox it shrinks to an axe-core gate.

C14.note: Proving changelog lines with tests is honest, but it is one more merge request bot beside security auto-fix and Renovate, with little Google Cloud and no strong scene.

C15.note: The package stage is rare, but the model's share is thin, the human moment is a non-event, and the demo is two columns of numbers.

C16.note: Builds the escape hatch (flag, alert, runbook line) and pays it off at 3am, a full arc from create to monitor. Lower because it is a merge request time code editor, and wiring Unleash flags from scratch is fragile.

C17.note: Good Google Cloud depth (Cloud Logging, Sensitive Data Protection), but reading production logs after a merge is the Proof of Fix mechanism moved into the security space, and the human moment is quiet.

C18.note: Complaints counted inside the flag cohort by code is fresh and uses Service Desk and feature flags deeply; it pairs naturally with Front Row. Lower if seeded tickets look staged or flag writes need a token we cannot store.

C19.note: Controls that rise while production is sick and fall back on their own is inventive governance, but it needs Maintainer or Premium settings and an eight-day fast-forward, and little moves in 30 seconds.

C20.note: 'You said you'd revisit' is a good line, but telling a clot from a normal change is fuzzy, writing the proper fix is hard, and it overlaps Loose Ends.

C21.note: A clear configure-stage chore with clean removal MRs, but flag cleanup tools already exist outside the hackathon and the scene is mild.

C22.note: The most original question in the pool on paper, but it needs many real incidents with metrics, and statistics on seeded history will not convince on video.

C23.note: Giving back upstream first is rare and kind, but the upstream fix must be staged with our own library and three weeks compressed, so the loop feels pretend.

C24.note: 'It is not you' is warm, but flaky tests sit next to CI fixers and it needs weeks of retries by several people.

C25.note: Uses Duo skills files, but GitLab already has a Review instructions learner flow that does this, LORE won February, and it touches two stages.

C26.note: Real GitLab pain (schedules that run as the person leaving, sole approvers, CODEOWNERS), and nobody in the field handles leaving. Lower because reading other people's settings may need Maintainer, and it is a checklist more than automation.

C27.note: Tight and real: drift read from Cloud Run with keyless auth, the fix written back in Clara's name, the next deploy stopped with a plain message. Lower if the drift check cannot start a flow without a person.

C28.note: A smart small feature at the moment of consent, but it is one question on an approval, three stages, and it needs Premium deployment approvals.

C29.note: Turns the three autonomy levels into a path, the exact theme question, which I like. Lower because the earned record must be seeded, and an autonomy budget is already BABYDOV's pitch.

C30.note: Kemi's postcard is sweet, but checking production a week after merge looks like Proof of Fix and June's Stayed Shipped, and it needs real telemetry.

C31.note: Uses GitLab's own governance records, but it sits next to the crowded evidence and receipts space, GitLab already has compliance reports, and the scene is a CSV.

C32.note: Real traffic decides, callers are told by name and removal waits in escrow, a complete arc with a school librarian at the end. Lower because fourteen quiet days must be compressed and seeded callers can look fake.

C33.note: Nice traceability (issue, MR, deployment per environment, flag strategy) with every claim checked by code, but it is a question tool for support; stronger folded into Front Row.

C34.note: Siobhan's mangled name is instant and filmable, and the migration runs on a copy with person-level diffs. Lower because the waiting production job is a familiar gate and a migration checker appeared in February.

C35.note: Asking why at the moment of the pin is clever, but the payoff is 'a year later', which must be staged, and it sits near organizational memory.

C36.note: Speaks to contributor success and Kwame's moment is memorable, but the post-code depth is thin and the created trigger on a revert MR is unverified.

C37.note: A planted canary person proving erasure after every release is original and opens compliance, a free space. Lower if several real stores on Google Cloud eat the build or the video leads with a release hold.

C38.note: Deep GitLab CI craft (generated child pipelines, a manual job per cue, protected environments, flag writes) with the person's go as the design, a strong Assisted entry. Lower if Duo only writes the cue file and the many moving parts break on camera.

C39.note: The theme turned around (how a person stops every pipeline, schedule and agent while she works) is my Most Creative dark horse. Lower because freezes and trigger toggles may need Maintainer and the agent only finds the isolation points.

C40.note: Well designed, with a go-around and a gate at the one-way step, but on video it is a release runner with an approval, the shape of my own reference project and BABYDOV.

C41.note: Merged but not delivered is a real lead time problem and the 'Hands!' call is fun, but it drifts toward stale merge request nudge bots.

C42.note: Hearback against live state beats a handoff summary, but it sits next to the banned handoff notes generator and needs two people on camera.

C43.note: The agent really runs runbook steps on staging and fixes the prose by MR, which is agentic and useful. Lower because restore drills need real backups and a tightly fenced staging, and the scene is a log.

C44.note: Small, sharp and rare: the customer confirms the exact rows and code refuses a mismatch (11 rows, 1 marked). Lower if the demo database and the support story feel thin.

C45.note: Comparing what each environment needs, by names and hashes only, solves a common outage, but it is a pre-promotion check and reads as one more gate.

C46.note: Gloria's phone-free holiday is touching, but counting performers needs months of history and the agent mostly writes scripts and schedules.

C47.note: The personal replies to everyone who wrote in are lovely, but judges will see an incident chatbot, which is excluded.

C48.note: Exercises the whole MR, pipeline, deploy and monitor loop several times and brings Mira's fix home; finding the bad change by elimination is clever. Lower if several deploy cycles do not fit in three minutes.

C49.note: Looking along time instead of code structure is a fresh post-merge angle, but judges may hear 'what could this break', and it needs real scheduled jobs and date logic.

C50.note: Starts from a marketer's issue and ends with load tests and scheduled Cloud Run capacity, a full arc across six stages. Lower if honest load tests cost too much or the scaled-down wave looks fake.

C51.note: An emergency lane with a never-skip list is sensible, but it is CI test selection, where CrossCut already won.

C52.note: One '@pause' that greys out every change in motion is a good scene, but it overlaps Lockout Tagout and needs freeze rights we may not have.

C53.note: Questioning green pipelines that needed a retry is a nice twist, but it sits next to CI fixers and needs hundreds of CI runs.

C54.note: Six real stages and a no-blame note to Felix, but secret detection is a crowded space and rotation needs credentials a flow cannot read.

C55.note: Clean hands-off framing, but it is a release gate with conditions plus auto-merge, the most crowded shape.

C56.note: Rating publishers and letting top patches flow to production is a real hands-off loop, but it lives beside security auto-fix and Renovate, with no human scene.

C57.note: Rare and humane: who was hurt and how we make it right, with numbers from code, a dry-run repair and a person's approval before anyone is contacted. Lower if the credit logic overshadows the GitLab automation.

top10.why: Bounded hands-off that is not a release gate: a person signs tonight's powers by merge, code enforces them, the phone stays dark; deep use of flags, Cloud Run and incidents.
The most GitLab-native human loop: Service Desk, a flag user list in production, the reporters' replies, a person widens, then a release; strong for Supervised.
Best 30 seconds in the pool and genuinely agentic (the model drives a keyboard like a screen reader user); a Most Creative contender if the browser runs inside the flow.
Nobody builds 'who was hurt and how do we make it right'; code sets the numbers, a dry-run repair goes through a protected environment, a person approves before contact.
Users' own words, counted inside the flag cohort by code, can hold the next rollout step; Service Desk plus feature flags, two open spaces.
The deepest GitLab CI craft here (generated child pipelines, a manual job per cue, protected environments, flags) with the human go as the design; strong for Assisted.
A real outage cause closed in a tight loop: drift read from Cloud Run with keyless auth, adopted in the fixer's name, the next deploy stopped with a plain message.
The agent experiments on no-traffic Cloud Run revisions so the woken engineer picks a tested fix; a credible Assisted story with natural Google Cloud use.
Small, rare and filmable: the customer confirms the exact rows and code refuses '11 rows, 1 marked'.
A canary person proves erasure after each release: an open compliance space, real Google Cloud stores, a strong human reason.

traps.why: Clever framing, but on video it is a release runner with an approval before the last step, the shape of the reference project and BABYDOV; it will be filed with the gatekeepers.
Answers the theme head on, but the earned record must be seeded or staged; six fake approvals read as theatre, and BABYDOV already pitches an autonomy budget.
The most original question in the pool, but control groups need many real incidents with metrics; statistics on seeded history will not convince.
The replay needs weeks of metrics and pages; seeded history makes the before and after chart look staged.
A week-later check of production will be filed with Proof of Fix and June's Stayed Shipped.
Same mechanism as Proof of Fix (read production logs after a merge), moved into the crowded security space.
GitLab already ships a Review instructions learner flow; judges will see a copy of a stock flow.
However kind the replies, it will be judged as the excluded incident chatbot.
Looks hands-off but is a gatekeeper with conditions plus auto-merge, the most crowded shape.

The whole night depends on starting flows from non-human alerts through the Flows API; if that is not accepted the night must be faked, and the agent never acts. C01 shares this start, so test it on day one and keep a trigger-token pipeline owned by the engineer as the fallback.
If a browser cannot run inside the Duo flow sandbox, the agent no longer explores and it shrinks to an axe-core CI job with a model summary, which is a smoke-test gate.

If demoed as a 'your bug is fixed' email it collides with the banned notifier and Proof of Fix; Service Desk email setup and flag writes from CI may need Maintainer. Lead with the reporters-first rollout.
Protected environment approval rules and deploy freezes need Maintainer or Premium; the fallback, a gate job reading a file, shows little GitLab. C39 and C52 share this risk.
Many moving parts across separate person-started flow runs; if Duo only writes the cue file, it is a manual-job pipeline with theatre words.
